label: Korean hunter / system web novel
description: Modern Korea with gates, ranked hunters and a system only the hero can see. Short punchy paragraphs, status windows, weak-to-strong progression, a hook at the end of every chapter.
voice: Short paragraphs: one to three sentences, often a single line. White space is part of the rhythm.
Close third person, past tense, on the protagonist unless the bible says otherwise. His inner voice is dry, understated and a little cold.
System messages sit on their own line in square brackets, terse and mechanical: [Quest complete.] [Strength +3] [A hidden condition has been met.] Never chatty.

Korean names keep the family name first (Kang Jin-Woo); after the first mention use the given name. Honorifics only where Koreans would use them: hyung, noona, sunbae, Director Choi, Guild Master Baek.
Show power through numbers, reactions and consequences: a stat change, a room going quiet, a guild calling back the same night.
Modern Korean texture: Seoul districts, subway lines, convenience-store kimbap, hagwons, part-time shifts, Hunter Association paperwork, news tickers about gate breaks.
End every chapter on a hook: a new notification, a reveal, an enemy stepping in, a rank being read aloud.

structure.guide: Open with the protagonist at the bottom: weakest rank, exploited or humiliated, inside a concrete dangerous situation. Make the gap between him and everyone else hurt.
structure.then: Show the new power's first small uses and its rules; the people who looked down on him still see nothing.

structure.guide: The system appears in a life-or-death moment: the first quest window, its absurd demand and its penalty. He survives by a hair.
structure.then: Train and level: each chapter gives one concrete gain (a skill, an item, a stat) and one person noticing he has changed.

structure.guide: His first fight won alone with the new power, with a visible reward and a cost nobody else understands.
Someone important sees what he can do: a guild scout, the Association, a top-rank hunter. Interest turns into pressure.
structure.then: Bigger gates, harder choices; his hidden class is at risk of being found out.

structure.guide: He faces the rival or the people who abandoned him and wins in a way that costs them face in public.
A truth about the system or the gates recasts everything: the power has an owner, a price or a purpose.
structure.then: He acts on the new truth; allies and enemies realign; the stakes grow from personal to national.

structure.guide: Something he could not prevent: an ally hurt, a gate breaking in the city, his secret leaking.
The big raid or gate break: the strongest enemy so far, the whole cast watching, every earlier upgrade paying off.
structure.then: Consequences land: rank re-evaluated, public reaction, the relationships move forward.

structure.guide: Close this arc and open the next: a larger threat, a new system message, a door that should not exist.

outline_guidance: Every chapter needs a gain or a loss the reader can count: a level, a skill, an item, money, a rank, or someone's respect. Chapters are short and end on a hook. No chapter is only a training montage or only talking.
outline_example: Ten Minutes | In the collapsing boss room Han Do-Yun drags Lee Ha-Eun behind a pillar while the stone knight hunts the survivors | A quest window only he can see orders him to survive ten minutes | The timer starts and the knight turns toward the pillar
scene_guidance: Open in motion, in a specific place.
At most one system window per scene unless the scene is about the system.
Let bystanders react: whispers, phones out, a guild scout making a call.
Fights stay readable: where everyone stands, what the move is, what it costs.
worldbuilding: Gates or dungeons ranked E to S, with a break timer and what happens when it runs out.
The Hunter Association and the big guilds as institutions with politics, contracts and money.
The system's rules: what it gives, what it demands, what failure costs.
Ordinary life under the gates: insurance, evacuations, damaged districts, hunter celebrities.
naming: Korean names, family name first: Kang, Choi, Yoo, Baek, Seo, Han, Park, Lee, Jung, Yoon, Cha, Go, with hyphenated two-syllable given names (Jin-Woo, Soo-Ah, Min-Jae, Ha-Eun). Guilds get strong names (White Tiger Guild, Reaper Guild).
sample:
The window opened while the others were still screaming.

[Daily Quest: Survive.]

Do-Yun read it twice. Then a third time, because the stone knight was walking toward him and his hands would not stop shaking.

[Time remaining: 09:58]

Behind him, someone was crying. In front of him, the knight raised its sword.

He did not run. There was nowhere left to run to.
